items.readable_text:
Content:
Consider the following sequence:
[MATH: 1,\quad 3,\quad 5,\quad 7,\quad 9,\quad \ldots]
Notice that the difference (or "jump") between two consecutive numbers is always the same.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/9a8b6d04df0ac9672785bb852bd71e77]

Content:
A sequence where the jump never changes is called an arithmetic sequence.

Content:
We call this jump the common difference, and represent it using the letter [MATH: d.] In this particular case, the common difference is [MATH: d=2.]

items.title: Finding a Common Difference

sections.normalized_html: What is the common difference of the following arithmetic sequence? [MATH: 7,\: 2,\: -3,\: -8,\: \ldots]
sections.readable_text:
What is the common difference of the following arithmetic sequence?
[MATH: 7,\: 2,\: -3,\: -8,\: \ldots]

sections.normalized_html:
The common difference [MATH: d] of an arithmetic sequence is the difference between any two consecutive terms.

Therefore, the common difference for our sequence is

[MATH: d|= a_{2} − a_{1}; = 2 − 7; = − 5.]

EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The common difference [MATH: d] of an arithmetic sequence is the difference between any two consecutive terms.

Therefore, the common difference for our sequence is

[MATH: d|= a_{2} − a_{1}; = 2 − 7; = − 5.]

items.title: Identifying an Arithmetic Sequence

sections.normalized_html:
Which of the three sequences below are arithmetic sequences?

  1. [MATH: 2, \: 4, \: 6, \: 8, \: \ldots]

  2. [MATH: 5, \: 2, \: -1, \: -4, \: \ldots]

  3. [MATH: 2, \: 5, \: 8, \: 12, \: \ldots]
sections.readable_text:
Which of the three sequences below are arithmetic sequences?

1. [MATH: 2, \: 4, \: 6, \: 8, \: \ldots]
2. [MATH: 5, \: 2, \: -1, \: -4, \: \ldots]
3. [MATH: 2, \: 5, \: 8, \: 12, \: \ldots]

sections.normalized_html:
To determine whether each sequence is an arithmetic sequence, we need to look at the jumps between terms in the sequence. If the jumps are the same, then they indeed represent a common difference of an arithmetic sequence.

  • In sequence I, the jumps are all the same. Therefore, sequence I is an arithmetic sequence with common difference [MATH: d=2.]

  • In sequence II, the jumps are all the same. Therefore, sequence II is an arithmetic sequence with common difference [MATH: d=-3.]

  • In sequence III, the jumps are not all the same. Therefore, sequence III is not an arithmetic sequence.

In conclusion, only sequences I and II are arithmetic sequences.

Item 6 — Example: Identifying an Arithmetic Sequence

Example Prompt:
Which of the three sequences below are arithmetic sequences?

1. [MATH: 2, \: 4, \: 6, \: 8, \: \ldots]
2. [MATH: 5, \: 2, \: -1, \: -4, \: \ldots]
3. [MATH: 2, \: 5, \: 8, \: 12, \: \ldots]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
To determine whether each sequence is an arithmetic sequence, we need to look at the jumps between terms in the sequence. If the jumps are the same, then they indeed represent a common difference of an arithmetic sequence.

- In sequence I, the jumps are all the same. Therefore, sequence I is an arithmetic sequence with common difference [MATH: d=2.]

- In sequence II, the jumps are all the same. Therefore, sequence II is an arithmetic sequence with common difference [MATH: d=-3.]

[IMG: /graphics/13da25d1fd5201bff9974d36439135c9]

- In sequence III, the jumps are not all the same. Therefore, sequence III is not an arithmetic sequence.

[IMG: /graphics/495007bf005470d02014354e810f7fda]

In conclusion, only sequences I and II are arithmetic sequences.
